channel.title: Acme: Daily Reading List
channel.description: Noteworthy articles from across the web.

item.title: WordPress developer roundup previews 7.2 and the latest Gutenberg changes
item.description: WordPress's September developer roundup covers changes in Gutenberg 23.8 and 23.9, practical tooling updates and the road to WordPress 7.2. Beta 1 is planned for late October and the final release for December, making this a useful early map of what plugin and theme developers should test.

item.title: Long-hidden Golden Age comic collection comes to auction
item.description: The newly surfaced Merrimack Valley Collection preserved major Golden Age comics for roughly 75 to 80 years. Its highlights include high-grade copies of Captain America Comics Nos. 1 and 3 and Batman's first nine issues—a rare original-owner time capsule from the formative superhero era.

item.title: ServiceNow folds its development environment into Studio
item.description: ServiceNow's September Creator update removes manual upgrades for its coding assistant and folds the ServiceNow IDE into Studio. The release also outlines features arriving with Brazil Early Availability, providing a concise look at how the platform's everyday development workflow is changing.

item.title: A forgotten box yields a Golden Age comics trove
item.description: The newly surfaced Merrimack Valley Collection spent 75 to 80 years in a cardboard box. Its exceptional Golden Age books include a 9.0 Captain America Comics No. 1, a 9.4 No. 3 containing Stan Lee's first Timely work, and Batman's first nine issues—eight graded 6.5 or higher.

item.title: Creative Commons meets Indigenous cultural authority
item.description: A new guide from Creative Commons and Local Contexts shows museums, archives and researchers how open licenses can work alongside Traditional Knowledge and Biocultural Labels. Case studies explain how the tools add provenance, community protocols and permissions that copyright alone cannot express.

item.title: St. Augustine dig finds its first British redoubt
item.description: A 15-foot-wide dry moat found in Lincolnville is the first physical evidence of one of seven British redoubts built around St. Augustine. The 1781 fortification survived only as marks on old maps until the city's archaeology program examined the lot before home construction and recovered thousands of plant remains.

item.title: Search summaries can help experience-based subreddits
item.description: A study of 105,012 subreddits finds that Google's static search summaries increased daily comments by 12% and active commenters by 12.4%, with the strongest gains in smaller communities centered on lived experience. More interactive search answers reduced that effect, offering a useful wrinkle for anyone building a forum around practical advice.

item.title: Patricia Highsmith's hidden years writing comic books
item.description: Before her novels made her famous, Patricia Highsmith worked for American Comics Group and freelanced in comics for about six years. Paul Gravett traces recurring ideas—secret identities, menacing terrain and lurid fantasy—from those scripts into her fiction, and notes that she even applied to write Wonder Woman in 1947.

item.title: Chicago comics history moves from page to gallery
item.description: The new Linework: Chicago Comics and Community exhibition explores the city's role as a center for contemporary comics. Built around the Linework anthology launched in 2010, it features artists including Ivan Brunetti and Nick Drnaso, whose Sabrina became the first graphic novel longlisted for the Booker Prize.

item.title: A practical roadmap to California publicity rights
item.description: This state-by-state legal guide maps California's overlapping statutory and common-law publicity rights. The statute is limited to name, voice, signature, photograph and likeness; the common-law claim can reach a broader persona. Its cases and postmortem-right details make it a useful starting point when reusing public-domain film.

item.title: Twenty million public-domain newspaper scans become a dataset
item.description: “American Stories” converts 20 million Library of Congress newspaper scans into article-level text using layout detection and optical character recognition. The openly described pipeline and dataset make historical reporting far easier to search and analyze than page images alone.

item.title: A snapshot of electronic science-fiction fandom
item.description: This archival “Dead Media Beat” traces electronic science-fiction fanzines and amateur press associations, from the Fantasy Amateur Press Association's origins to EAPA's online experiments. It is a compact piece of publishing history about how fan communities adapted their mailing-and-comment culture to networks.

item.title: Betty Boop, Blondie and three classic detectives enter the public domain
item.description: Works first published in 1930 are now free of U.S. copyright, including early Betty Boop and Blondie appearances, nine Mickey Mouse cartoons and the book debuts of Nancy Drew, Sam Spade and Miss Marple. The annual release offers a rich field for copyright archaeology, preservation and new editions—while later character elements can remain protected.

item.title: Russian strikes put Ukraine's independent publishers at risk
item.description: Russian attacks have destroyed more than 13 million Ukrainian books and crucial printing infrastructure, including eight million books at publisher Ranok's warehouse. Small presses and debut authors are especially exposed, making proposed grants, state purchases and war-risk insurance consequential for literary diversity and cultural survival.

item.title: What WordPress's release scanning catches—and what it cannot
item.description: WordPress.org now scans each plugin and theme release during a cooldown and blocks high-risk updates before distribution. This practical guide explains the boundary that matters: the gate can examine a new release, but it cannot protect an already installed vulnerable or compromised plugin. It then maps the remaining site-owner defenses.
